utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. And I'd like to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Ms. Marcus, you would like to make a submission.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. On the 15th of November, 2011, the Chamber denied the Stanisic Defence motion to tender the Milosevic testimony and associated exhibits of Witness DST-071 pursuant to Rule 92 bis, ordering that he be called for cross-examination. The Defence's original 92 bis motion on the 26th of September included the witness's Milosevic, Brdjanin, and Tadic testimony. However, in an e-mail on the 11th of October the Stanisic Defence informed the Prosecution that they did not intend to tender the testimony from the Brdjanin and Tadic cases and they only intended to tender the Milosevic testimony. This was confirmed in the corrigendum that the Defence filed on the 13th of October, 2011. According to the corrigendum, the Defence would be tendering approximately 190 pages of testimony from the Milosevic case and more than 500 pages of associated exhibits. Yesterday, the Stanisic Defence informed the Prosecution that they will, contrary to their prior submissions, seek to tender through Witness DST-071 an additional approximately 400 pages of the witness's prior testimony from the Brdjanin and Tadic cases and that they will inform us today of the pages they will seek to tender from the Stanisic/Zupljanin and the Krajisnik cases. They also informed us that they will also be tendering the exhibits discussed during these portions which are associated to that prior testimony. The Prosecution submits that the testimony of DST-071 in this case should be limited to the 92 ter confirmation process for the Milosevic testimony and associated exhibits as per the Defence corrigendum of the 13th of October, 2011, and to cross-examination by the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any wish to already respond, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd like to think about it, then we'll hear --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I can say this at this stage, Your Honour: That we are going through the testimony looking for ways to reduce the notice we provided to the Prosecution. We have no wish to overload the Court. Much of the testimony is duplicative and we're going to remove that duplication. And once we've done that, the amount that the Prosecution are complaining about will be significantly less, and they will have, in our submission, plenty of time to deal with it. The issues that the witness is going to deal with are straightforward. But we understand the Prosecution's complaints, and we're going to do what we can to reduce the workload of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that the parties are not yet got stuck, at least as far as the Stanisic Defence is concerned. Let's wait for a second to see what they come up with. Ms. Marcus, but you felt a bit intimidated by the announcement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's not only the quantity. It's also that they first noticed a great deal of testimony, then two months ago they informed us that they wouldn't be tendering that. So there was no further work done on that and it was not part of their application. Now, before the witness is being called, being called only for cross-examination following an application under 92 bis - this was an original 92 bis witness - so now the witness is a 92 ter witness, and to add -- to double the amount of material, I mean, when we applied for 92 bis for some of our witnesses, we were denied and we called them. We may have added a few individual documents, but essentially they're converting the witness to a heavily viva voce witness, which we feel is not only an issue of notice and preparation, but also an issue which goes contrary to their prior applications and to the Chamber's order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that the Stanisic Defence is seeking ways to make the witness lose some weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. But I would remind the Prosecution about their objection to this witness being 92 bis. In short, it's what the witness hasn't commented on which is the problem for the Prosecution. They say, Well, the witness was never asked about the Red Berets, he was never asked by Mr. Stanisic, he was never asked about supply by the DB. So the idea that the witness can now come into court and the Defence doesn't have a job to do viva voce is inconsistent with their original position. The idea that we could call the witness, put the statements in, and then let the Prosecution do that work, it's simply not reasonable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Interesting discussion. We'll move on. I do understand that there was also a submission. The Chamber, of course, will consider both the developments and the submission you made, Ms. Marcus. I do understand that there was some information about the video. Was that the 1995 video? Or was it the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the 1991 video.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On yesterday's transcript, at page 16325, the Simatovic Defence played 65 ter 2D1017.1. After playing the video, the Chamber requested further information concerning the contextual information about when this funeral occurred. The Prosecution was able to obtain the following information: General Mladen Bratic of the Yugoslav People's Army was killed during combat operations on 4 November 1991 in Vukovar while he was assigned to Operational Group North. General Bratic's funeral was held on a date between the 6th and 8th of November, 1991, in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, we can confirm that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. There's agreement on the date of the death and the funeral of General Bratic. If there's nothing else, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Bakrac, you announced yesterday that you would need, as we find it on the transcript, one hour and a half. That's how it was translated to us. But you actually said, if I may believe those who are native B/C/S speakers, that you said one and a half to two hours. Now, you've used two hours and 24 minutes until now, which means that asking now for two hours would bring you well beyond what you asked for originally, that was four hours. Can you try to see whether you can finish in, well, let's say, if possible, in a little bit over one hour and a half. Try to do your utmost best.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll do my best to complete my examination in an hour and a half, but I would be grateful if you would grant me a little extra time, if really necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said, a little bit over one hour and a half would be fine with the Chamber. Good morning, Mr. Pelevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, we'll continue. But before doing so, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday, that is, that you'll speak the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac will now continue his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Pelevic.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, yesterday we spoke about a situation in which a group of citizens together with Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, obtained five seats at the first elections held. And as yesterday we were explaining that at the time Serbia was a part of the federal entity, together with Montenegro. So that everything is clear, I'd like to ask you whether these seats were obtained in the Assembly of Serbia or in the Assembly of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the Assembly of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pelevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would now like to have a look at a video-clip that might shed some light. The number is 2D1012.1. There won't be any sound and we'll see three short extracts. It's V003118. It's a Prosecution document. There's a commentary from the Croatian television which we haven't transcribed which is why it's necessary to have a look at it without any sound. Could we please see 2D1012 from 42 minutes, 02 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, please look at the video and tell us what sort of a gathering is being held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have a look at 42 minutes and 25 seconds up to 42 minutes, 46 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we now have a look at the clip from 43:31 to 43, 58 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, now that we have frozen the image, could you tell us -- this image, in fact, is an at 43 minutes and 58 seconds. You can see three individuals. There's one person in the background. Can you tell us who this person is, if you recognise him, from the left to the right?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, the image is very obscure, very dark on my screen. Could it please be made a little lighter? because I can't see anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may also be a matter of adjusting the angle of the -- under which the witness looks at.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now is better. Now is better. Thank you. [Interpretation] To the left we can say the late president of Serbia, Slobodan Milosevic. In the middle we have the then-president of Montenegro, Momir Bulatovic. And to the right we have the president of Yugoslavia, Mr. Dobrica Cosic. And in the background, I can recognise myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, could you tell me what the nature of this gathering is and when it was held?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting was held in 1993. I believe it was in the spring, but I cannot remember the exact date. I see I still have a bandage because I was still being treated for the wounds that I received in Velebit. It has to do with opening the Sava centre in Belgrade. That was the subject of the meeting. The meeting convened officials from all the Serbian territories from Serbian -- Serbia, Montenegro, Republika Srpska, and the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and I think that the members of parliament from those areas, those countries, participated at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could 2D1012.1 please be marked for identification for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, we have no objection to what's been played so far. Though I don't know if there's additional portions that Mr. Bakrac plans on adding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any additional portions, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I just want to ask Mr. Pelevic whether he saw officials from Republika Srpska and Republic of Serbian Krajina as well.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that the image was very obscure. The only person I could recognise was Biljana Plavsic. Perhaps we could have a look at it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, is there any dispute about that Mrs. Plavsic appears on one of these videos? Okay, let's then not look --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- any further. Madam Registrar, the number for the document -- for the video would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Video number 2D1012.1 will receive number D656, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, yesterday you said that at one point in time the Serbian Volunteer Guard was resting. It wasn't disbanded, but it was, so to speak, resting; it was passive. Could you tell us when it was activated, if it was, and what the reason for this was?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbian Volunteer Guard was activated sometime in November 1994 when our instructors left for Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, before we move on to a more specific question about that, tell me, did Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and the Serbian Volunteer Guard send some offers to anybody before they were eventually engaged? And if that was the case, who did they send their offers to?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In agreement with the president of the Party of Serbian Unity, Mr. Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, I sent a letter to the president of Republika Srpska, Mr. Radovan Karadzic. In that letter I wrote that we are at the disposal of the Republika Srpska should our assistance be necessary and should the assistance of both the Serbian Volunteer Guard and the Serbian Party of Unity be necessary if the Republic of Serbian -- of -- if the Republika Srpska came under attack. And there were such suggestions on the part of Muslims and the NATO pact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Before I put to you a few other questions, let's look at 2D1009.1 from 46.49 seconds to 47 minutes .43 seconds. Let us wait for the booths to locate the transcript 2D1009.1. And while we're waiting for this to appear, this is part of the Prosecutor's 0000268.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... Mr. Bakrac, could I seek clarification of one of the -- of, as a matter of fact, the last answer. You said: " -- if the Republika Srpska came under attack. And there were such suggestions on the part of Muslims and the NATO pact." Did you intend to say that the Muslims and the NATO pact suggested that there might be attacks on Republika Srpska; or did you intend to say that there were suggestions that the Muslims or the NATO pact would attack the Republika Srpska? Which of the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said it clearly. There were such indications about the intentions of Croatian and Muslim forces to attack the Republika Srpska with the support of NATO forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the suggestions were that - and now the answer is even more complete - that Croatia or the Muslims would attack with the support of NATO forces. Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. And now let's look at 2D1009.1.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "You have recently visited many cities in Republika Srpska and the Republic of Serbian Krajina. When it comes to the Party of Serbian Unity, in how many areas are you present? "We are present in Republic of Serbian Krajina almost everywhere. In Republika Srpska, I come to Bijeljina every week. I'm also present in Banja Luka and have visited Prijedor and Doboj several times. However, we have not had the media coverage, but we will start doing that as well in the future we believe we are involved in a sufficient number of humanitarian operations. But let me repeat, we are always ready to help militarily. "When there was a crisis in Gorazde recently, I sent a personal letter to President Karadzic and placed the Serbian Volunteer Guard, said if I need to mobilize them again and put them under the command of the Army of Republika Srpska, I would be willing to help those people. However, I know that this wasn't necessary. "Too many armies is not a good thing because there are more casualties in that case. I believe the masses of armed people in Republika Srpska are sufficient, not only to stop the Muslims and Ustashas but to liberate the territories that are presently under the control of Muslims and Ustashas."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Pelevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, we heard what Mr. Raznjatovic said. He said that he had sent a letter and that he was willing to place himself under the command of the Army of Republika Srpska if such a need arose. And now let us look at something else. You said that you also sent a personal letter. Let us look at D29, which is already in evidence. While we're waiting for this document to appear on the screen, let us say that it was sent on the 16th of April, 1994. It says here: "To the president of Republika Srpska, Mr. Radovan Karadzic. The Serbian Volunteer Guard and the Party for Serbian Unity support your heroic resistance against NATO and the USA ... "As always, with all available forces we are ready to join the army forces of Republika Srpska in order to protect Serbian nationality and Orthodoxy. "The 16th of April, 1994." Were those the two letters, i.e., the two times you addressed President Karadzic; once, it was done by you, the other time by Mr. Karadzic when you -- you have told us that you also sent a letter to President Karadzic and placed yourself at his disposal?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I did the technical part of the job. The letter was signed by Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, the president of the Serbian Party of Unity. I drafted a letter and I sent it; however, the person who actually sent it was Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. So we're talking one and the same letter. There were no two letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I go on, I would like to tender 2D1009, and I would like it to be MFI'd for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 2D1009.1 will be receive number D657, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, first of all tell me, since you participated in the drafting of this letter, did you previously use Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, or the Serbian Volunteer Guard -- did you previously have to obtain somebody's approval for placing yourself under -- on -- at the disposal of President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Why should we have done that? We were independent and we could act independently of anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you went to the Republika Srpska as the Serbian Volunteer Guard, did you have your own command? How did the whole thing function when you fought in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, we could not fight there independently. We were under the command of the Army of Republika Srpska and partly of the MUP of Republika Srpska, i.e., of the police of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pelevic. And now let us go back to something else. You said that in November the Serbian Volunteer Guard was reactivated and engaged once again. Can you tell us how that came -- came about?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime in early November Zeljko Raznjatovic and I had offices next to each other in the party headquarters. The assistant of defence minister, Mile Milanovic, also known as Mrgud, came to our headquarters and he told us that a meeting had been held the previous day. The meeting was attended by Slobodan Milosevic, the president of Serbia; Radovan Karadzic, the president of Republika Srpska; and Milan Martic, the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina; as well as Fikret Abdic, who was the leader of Muslims from the Cazin Krajina and a well-known businessman. He told us that at the meeting it had been agreed that a group of instructors should be sent and that they would be training the military troops of Fikret Abdic in the Cazin Krajina. Why was that a topical issue? Because Mr. Fikret Abdic wanted to join Republika Srpska, i.e., he wanted the Cazin Krajina, which was in Western Bosnia, to be merged with the Republic of Serbian Krajina so that Serbs and Muslims could live together. That agreement had been reached and Mr. Mrgud told us that we discussed -- they discussed who could train Fikret Abdic's forces in the Krajin Cazina [as interpreted]. Milan Martic was asked to send some of the troops of the Republic of Serbian Krajina to do that, i.e., the best of his instructors. That's how it was agreed that the instructors of the Serbian Volunteer Guard who were the most experienced and seasoned men should go there. This was told to us by Mr. Milan Milanovic, Mrgud.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Was -- did that come to fruition? Didn't Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, accept that -- was that an order by Mrgud, or a suggestion? What could we call that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since Milan Milanovic, Mrgud, was an assistant minister of defence of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, we understood that as an effective order, and we acted upon that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know whether there was random selection of men or was there a list with the chosen men?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that the selection was not done randomly. It was an important mission which was headed by the then-centre -- commander of the centre of the Serbian Volunteer Guard, Milorad Ulemek, Legija. He was a colonel in the Serbian Volunteer Guard. He issued an order to the technical service in the headquarters of the party of Serbian unity and the SDG headquarters in Belgrade to call some of -- some 70 of the most seasoned fighters and trainers who could train Fikret Abdic's forces. The service did that. And if I remember correctly, some 50 to 70 people eventually went to Velika Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know how they went there? How did they travel from Belgrade to Velika Kladusa?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, they were instructed to come to Erdut, and from there they went to the Republic of Serbian Krajina -- I apologise, to Republika Srpska, i.e., to the Cazin Krajina which was then a part of Bosnia-Herzegovina which didn't belong to anybody. It was Fikret Abdic's turf. He was surrounded by the forces of the 5th Corps of the Muslim army that wanted to annex that part to the Muslim and Croatian Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Those individuals who went to Erdut, did they leave their IDs, jewellery, and personal belongings in the party headquarters?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When the -- these individuals were called up, and you say that eventually about 50 people left, did these individuals report to the headquarters of the Serbian Volunteer Guard in Belgrade before they travelled?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And did they leave their personal effects in Ljutice Bogdana Street in the headquarters of the Serbian Volunteer Guard? Did they leave their -- behind their IDs, jewellery, and personal belongings?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Party of Serbian Unity was not a bank. We did not have a vault where people could leave their belongings behind. Of course not. They came to the party headquarters and the SDG headquarters in civilian clothes. They would board vans and leave for Erdut. That was all. Nobody had IDs on them. The only thing that they had were their membership cards for the SDG. They could not leave anything behind. There was no room for that. We did not have a vault or any other capacities for anybody to leave their personal belonging behind. That was not a commonplace things to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, you have just told us that they did not have their IDs on them but that, rather, they had been provided with SDG membership cards. Why didn't they have IDs? Was it so to make it impossible for anybody to know where they had come from and where they resided?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a rule of the SDG. Everybody had to leave their SDG membership cards behind in the headquarters. And when they went to -- or Erdut, they took their membership cards because upon return from Erdut nobody was allowed to take those SDG membership cards because of some abuses that had happened beforehand. That was the rule that was well established. Nobody who wore civilian clothes was allowed to have their SDG membership cards on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: At the battle-field in the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the Republika Srpska, did you bear the Tiger emblems that the SDG could be identified by?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just stop you for a second. Why not invite the witness to answer the last question? You were asked why they didn't have their IDs. You gave a perfect answer on why they had the SDG identity cards, but you didn't answer the question. The question was: Why did they not have their IDs with them? Could you please answer that question. And, Mr. Bakrac, I take it that you -- if put a question, that you would like to receive an answer to it. But apparently you accepted an answer on what seems to be a different question. Could you tell us why they were supposed not to take their IDs with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in war, one does not have one's ID, although that was the principle of the old Serbian army. We followed that principle in the SDG. We had ID cards of the SDG in the battle-field, and these cards had all the information that IDs had, the name, place of birth, date of birth, and all other essential characteristics. And there was also photographs. It wasn't necessary for the men to have identity cards because the SDG cards were quite sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Same information on that card. What is then the principle that you shouldn't take your ID, whereas you take another card which contains exactly the same information? Or was there additional information on the SDG cards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The SDG cards didn't have the ID card number and the date of issue of the ID card or the place where the ID cards were issued, but other information was there. Let me just inform you that it wasn't forbidden to have your ID card on you. But this was the practice that was followed, the principle. It wasn't that important for us. But as a rule, the men had SDG cards on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now, when travelling to the headquarters before being sent to Erdut, were they without IDs then? Did they arrive at the headquarters in Belgrade without any idea -- ID card and would then be provided with their SDG cards? Or ... how did they do that on their way to the headquarters in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As a rule, anyone could go to the HQ with their ID cards. But generally speaking, we all left our ID cards at home, and the cards that we had left in -- in the SDG headquarters in Belgrade were -- would be cards that we would use to go with to Erdut, to the staff there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, let's just clarify this as much as possible. As far as the SDG membership cards are concerned, did these cards contain information on the men's blood group?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's quite natural. Because of the possibility of being wounded and because of the necessity of providing first aid on site during a battle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And the ID cards that the authorities issued at the time, did they contain such information on blood groups?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These were old ID cards. The new ID cards contained such information, but that was after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you were on the battle-field, did you always bear this identifiable Tiger emblem?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, the SDG was well-known. As the SDG, it went by that name. But it was better known as the Tigers. So on one side we had the SDG insignia, and on the other sleeve, on the other arm, the Tigers insignia. But when we came part of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and that was always the case -- but in 1993 I think we also had the insignia of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. We had that insignia on the sleeve, either by the Tiger insignia or perhaps without the Tiger insignia there, and on our berets there was also the insignia the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. It was embroidered. The Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. It wasn't a metal insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, since we're dealing with this now -- I was going to take a look at this later, but since we're dealing with this now, you provided us with several photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a look at 2D1040, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, you seem to be the person in the photograph. Can you tell us what these two emblems are on your left shoulder and our your beret?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a photograph of me. I assume that it was towards the end of 1993. It wasn't possible to have photographs taken up until May or June. The beret has a badge sewn on. It says the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. And on my sleeve, below the Tigers badge, you can see the insignia of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. And then there are two medals of mine, and my rank. It's not a great photograph, but we won't go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could this photograph be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Could we have a closer look at the badge on the beret. And perhaps zoom in on it. You say, Mr. Pelevic, that it says: The Army of the Republic of Serbia Krajina. I have difficulties in finding any text on that emblem. Where is that text found?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, usually the berets don't have any writing on them, but the emblem is the same as the emblem on my sleeve. So it is the badge that belongs to the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Please have a look at the sleeve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you say, "Text is on the sleeve and the same emblem is found on the beret," that's what I understand. But to say that the emblem on the beret says Army of the -- that seems not to be very accurate.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2D1040 will receive number D658, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Since we are dealing with this subject matter, could we see 2D1038, please, which is another photograph that you provided us with. Could you please tell us who can be seen in the photograph and where the photograph was taken? We'll also comment on the board that we can see behind you. Could you please tell us who these two men in the photograph are.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the left you can see myself. And to the right you can see Milorad Ulemek, Legija, the commander of the army. And the board says the Serbian Army, Assault Battalion, Tigers. We could be identified by that name "Tigers" as well. As I have said, at the time we were an assault battalion of the Serbian Army of Krajina. The photograph was taken in Erdut in our training centre, and I cannot provide you with the exact date. I can't remember the date. I think it was in the year 1993, but I'm not completely sure. It couldn't have been earlier because we had a board on which it said the 101st Training Centre of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I suggest that this photograph also be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just based on the witness's answer we did have some confusion about what exactly the sign says and whether or not it includes the word "Krajina." We don't have a translation available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The sign? The board?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Correct. I believe the witness said it and then he added something, but we were -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It says "Srpska Vojska," the Serbian army, and then the name of a battalion. And then it read "Tigrovi." That's -- unless you would like to ... I think further down you see the emblem of a tiger with again the word "Tigrovi" on it. Do you find anything else on this apart from the four S's at the top? I understood the witness to explain all of the text, even literally. "Assault battalion," that's the seconds line. "Tigers" is the third line in yellow. And then the emblem is -- Do you find any other text which needs an explanation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No. We were just in -- we apologise if it's just our confusion. We were just a little bit confused by the answer. If that's the case, that's fine. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think that Mr. Bakrac wanted to have it admitted into evidence. Any objections? No objections. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2D1038 will receive number D659, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Yes, Mr. Pelevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in relation to the question put by the Prosecution, could the usher please show the insignia on my sleeve where you can see the very same insignia, and it says the "Serbian Army of Krajina." So that explains everything. Because it couldn't have been any other army. That other army was the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And here you can quite clearly see that it is called the "Serbian Army," because the Army of Yugoslavia was never called the Serbian Army. So you can see that it's the Serbian Army of Krajina. You can see that on the badge on my sleeve. I do apologise if I have interrupted you with this comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I tried -- that's the reason why I took some time. I tried to zoom in on the badge on your sleeve. And to be honest, I couldn't decipher any text there, but it's too vague for me. And you say, You can clearly see. Well, I do not know what I could clearly see, which I apparently fail to see. Could we zoom in, in great detail. Yes. Now, where is clearly visible the text you just mentioned? You may have a recollection that it's there, but ... if you say, "You can clearly see," then I wonder where I could see that. I see, as a matter of fact, which resembles very much the head of a tiger, rather than anything else. And that's guessing. That's guessing already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's not the head of a tiger. It's the Serbian coat of arms that was seen in the previous clip on my uniform. The emblem is the same. Unfortunately, you can't see the letters here because it was dark. I can't see the letters. But as you have said, I was able to recognise the badge that I wore. So it's a two-headed eagle, not a tiger's head. And there are crossed swords on the emblem too, and above it should say the "Serbian Army" and below it should say "Krajina," as was the case on the other badge that we previously saw. You can compare the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at the other badge and try to remember this one clearly. The previous one. The centre of the emblem is orange. Are you telling us, Mr. Pelevic, that the emblem we just saw on your shoulder is the same as the one below here? Yes, the centre is, to some extent, yellow. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, let's now have a look at 2D131. It's a newspaper article from "Novosti" dated the 9th of June, 2009. You had a look at the board which says -- on which you can see the inscription "assault battalion."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm just going read out part of this, Your Honour. It's the fourth paragraph. The fourth paragraph. In the B/C/S version it's at the bottom, and it's the fifth one, the fifth paragraph -- or, rather, the fifth column at the top in the B/C/S version. Could we just go to the right. Yes, there it is. It seems to be an interview with Mr. Milanovic, Mrguda [phoen]. "The Defence of the Slavonia and Baranja region depended on five brigades: The Denzka [phoen], the Vukovar one, the Mirkovac Brigade, the Beli Manastir Brigade, and the Dalj Brigade. We also had two independent battalions. Arkan's Serbian -- Serbian Volunteer Guards and the Skorpions. They were all officially under the command of the Eleventh Corps of the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, which for a certain period of time was under the command of Colonel Bogdan Sladojevic and then under the command of General Dusan Loncar." Mr. Pelevic, having seen these photographs and the assault battalion, we see the interview with Mr. Mrguda who says that there was an independent battalion in Arkan's SDG. Is it true that you were under the command of the Army of Republika Srpska and under the command of Bogdan Sladojevic and then under the commander of Dusan Loncar, General Dusan Loncar?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. It's the second page in the English version. I apologise for not informing you of the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, is it correct that you were under the Army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and that the person -- or the body in charge for the area was the 11th Corps under the command of the individual whom I just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. However, I don't want you to compare us with that unit whose name was Skorpions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That's what -- that's precisely what I was going to ask you. Did you have anything to do with them? Did you participate in combat with them?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. As far as I know, they guarded some oil fields. We did not have any contact with them. And it is good that that was the case, since they comprised the entire Serbian army during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just bear with me for a moment, I need to check something. I would like to tender 2D131 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2D131 will receive number D660, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm looking at the clock. 75 minutes short of half a minute are behind us, and maybe this is a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Bakrac. We'll take a break. And we resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I give you an opportunity to continue, Mr. Bakrac, I'd like to briefly revisit the matter of DST-071 and the package the Defence intends to -- to present under Rule 92 ter. The Chamber has considered it. Ms. Marcus, in view of the position taken by the Prosecution, the Defence is entitled to ask questions beyond what is found in the 92 bis, the initial 92 bis application. I mean, when I say "initial," it's the one limited to one testimony. At the same time, so, the Chamber has no problems in you going beyond that as -- in response to what the -- what -- what the Prosecution took as its position. But the Chamber has great difficulties with the way in which that's done. That is, again through expanding the 92 ter materially enormously, with all the associated exhibits, which are rather bulky exhibits. Therefore, the Chamber will hear any evidence beyond what is already found in the 92 bis application with the one testimony, hear it through an examination viva voce by the Stanisic Defence. Now, I can imagine that where the Prosecution says, "We'd like to cross-examine the witness on A, B, C, and D," that you take that as some guidance as to what you want to deal with as a subject matter for your further examination-in-chief going beyond 92 bis. So, therefore, the Chamber is still -- the portion you have presented in your 92 bis application, which was denied to the extent that the witness has to be called for cross-examination, that, approximately 190 pages of testimony, transcript of testimony, the Chamber accepts that as the basis for the evidence but insists on anything beyond that to be presented as viva voce testimony rather than as a bulky and most likely repetitious in many respects, et cetera, bulky material under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is the position we were moving to, to be honest, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then, of course, we'd like to hear from you what time you had on your mind you would need for that, and then we'll consider that as well. Because apparently what you presented as 92 bis, you consider that to be clear enough even without any further questions to be admitted into evidence. I can imagine that if the Prosecution was to cross-examine on that, that you want to elaborate a bit more, but you may have noticed that some other Chambers, 92 ter means 15 or 20 minutes in addition to that, but not hours and hours, and that's ... But, here again, for anything beyond what is found in that one testimony, there, of course, the Chamber finds there's -- that there's merit in your submission, that if the Prosecution wants to cross-examine on that, that you should have more time, although not through 92 ter, but a larger opportunity to elicit that evidence in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And, well, two things, Your Honour. Our approach is going to be to see what the witness knows and to examine him in direct to show that he doesn't know about Mr. Stanisic or the DB and he should do, if the Prosecution case was correct. So that's going to be our approach. I can't imagine that I'll be more than three hours, and I hope to be significantly less. And it's -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- perhaps you also carefully listen to Ms. Marcus on what matters she things cross-examination is vital so that you -- that you know you can be focussed in your further examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And I should say this, and this is as much for Madam Registrar as anyone else: That we've already given the witness a B/C/S transcript of the Milosevic case, so I think we're -- that's one of the problems that now which is no longer a problem, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we are moving forward. And I appreciate the understanding of the parties for the Chamber's position, and the Chamber tries to fully under the position of the parties when making any rulings or suggestions. Mr. Pelevic, our apologies for dealing with other matters. But we had to move forward with this as quickly as we can, and, therefore, you were the victim; you had to wait for a few minutes. Mr. Bakrac, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, before the break we spoke about the engagement of a number of your members in the Cazin Krajina and Velika Kladusa. Do you know how those people travelled from Belgrade to Erdut?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had two vans. I suppose that they travelled in those two vans. I'm not sure about that. However, I'm sure that they travelled in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know whether SDG members, those who were sent there, were remunerated? Were they compensated for their engagement?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They received per diems. At that time, the time of hyper-inflation, those were very low, but they could pay for their cigarettes, refreshments, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know how they received the monies due to them?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Milan Milanovic, Mrgud, told me and Arkan that their expenses would be covered by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the name of the company.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what was agreed at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know where they received the monies due to them?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I believe the transcript's incomplete with the witness's answer, lines 17 and 18 of page 31.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I -- you said, witness: "Mrgud told me and Arkan that their expenses would be covered by --" And could you then repeat by whom or by what.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By Mr. Fikret Abdic, who actually spear-headed the initiative to have his men in Velika Kladusa trained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It was mainly to correct the incomplete transcript. Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, during the Velika Kladusa mission did you receive any money in the party headquarters and the SDG headquarters in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Unfortunately we never received any money, either before or thereafter. Before the mission, during the mission, or after the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can we go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, you've told us that your members went there as instructors. Did you suffer any losses during that mission? And when I say "you," I mean the SDG. Was anybody wounded?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, it was not a battle mission. It was just a training exercise for the Muslim soldiers of Fikret Abdic. There were no actions or combat. But we did have two casualties; two soldiers hit an ambush when -- when they were on their way from the centre to a unit of Fikret Abdic. As far as I know, nobody was ever wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of those who had been killed?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. They were my good friends. One was Dimitrije Jasek, also known as Mita, and the other was my driver, Jugoslav Micic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, now we will move on to the summer of 1995. My question is this: Do you know if SDG members participated in combats on Mount Treskavica in the Trnovo theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was engaged and how?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A small detachment of the SDG under the command of Lieutenant Dragan Petrovic, Kajman [phoen], who unfortunately died in 1998. He succumbed to the wounds that he suffered during the war. I will now share with you what I heard from my commander. He said that he had met with Milan Milanovic, Mrgud, and Radovan Stojicic, Badza. I repeat, Badza and Arkan were friends. At that time Badza was already an assistant minister of the MUP in charge of public security. Badza told him that he had been asked by Radovan Karadzic in Trnovo theatre of war. Since the Dayton peace negotiations were coming up, he said that Serbia couldn't do much about that. And then the commander came with Milan Milanovic into his office. He invited me to join them. And I was present when Milan Milanovic asked Arkan to help him out. I believe that the situation was very difficult in view of the peace negotiations that were coming up. That same afternoon, Radovan Karadzic called. I was in Arkan's office when that telephone rang, and he asked him to send some of his guards to Trnovo and to place them under the command of Dragomir Milosevic, the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. And I believe that that was the breaking point, and it was then that the commander decided that our unit should go to Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pelevic. Now this has been corrected. Let us now look at 2D1032. This is a photo that was provided to us by yourself. Could you please comment upon it? Can you describe the event for us, and can you tell who the persons depicted in the photo are?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the photo be zoomed in a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: First of all let us see from left to right. Who are the persons depicted in this photo?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took the photo myself in Erdut. This is the lineup of the unit that was sent to Trnovo. On the left-hand side we see Commander Arkan who is inspected -- inspecting the lineup. In the middle -- centre, you see Mr. Milan Milanovic, Mrgud, the assistant minister of the MUP. On the right-hand side is Dragan Petrovic, Kajman, who was in command of that unit and that's why he attended the unit lineup. In the background you can see General Marko Pejic, also known as Peja. It was in charge of the Bosnian and Herzegovinian theatre of wear, i.e., he was responsible for what was going on in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did Marko Pejic go to the theatre of war?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only officer who went there was Dragan Pejovic, Kajman [phoen], and a sergeant whose name I can't remember. And Mihajlo, Zelko Raznjatovic, Arkan's, son also went. And he was even wounded there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I would like to tender the photo into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2D1032 will receive number D661, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, do you happen to know that Franko Simatovic, also known as Frenki, played a role in sending out that unit to Treskavica, to Trnovo, under Kajman's command?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. Why would he have played a role in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, did there come a time when you did go to Trnovo to visit that unit?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the death of our three volunteers, Commander Arkan ordered me to go there to see what had happened and to visit our volunteers. I was accommodated in Jahorina hotel. I spent a night there. And as soon as I arrived, I went to Trnovo and I talked to Lieutenant-Colonel Kajman. Arkan's son Mihajlo was also there. He was already wounded. He had suffered a slight injury. So I did go and visit them, and I learned that they were wounded from artillery fire of the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: While you were on Mount Jahorina that one day, did you notice that there was a headquarters, a staff there? Did you perhaps hear that a certain Franko Simatovic, Frenki, was in that staff?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there for two days. I spent just one night there. And I did not notice anybody. And truth be told, I did not even know Franko Simatovic. In any case, one thing is certain: There was no headquarters or staff in Jahorina hotel. I was met by the hotel manager. They were very polite and fair to me, but there was no staff in that hotel. The staff was in Pale. There were two staffs there. One belonged to the Army of Republic of Serbian Krajina under the command of General Dragomir Milosevic, and the staff of the Republika Srpska MUP under the command of the Defence Minister Tomislav Kovac. In other words, both staffs were in Pale. I did not see anything on Mount Jahorina, nor did anybody tell me anything about any activities might have been taking place there. The only thing that was happening in the hotel was the provision of hotel services, accommodation and food.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, now I'm going to show you -- Mr. Pelevic, did you have any communication with Trnovo when you were in the staff of the SDG?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When I say "communication," I mean telephone lines.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we mean the same thing. Lieutenant-Colonel Kajman came to the hotel and from there he could call the staff, and that's how we learned about the death of our three volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let us be very clear: Was that telephone line with Belgrade or with Erdut?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, let us now look at P1457. Mr. Pelevic, this is a telegram issued by the chief of the Security Services Centre in Srbanje [phoen], Rade Radovic, describing the events that happened on the 5th of July, 1995. First of all, I would like to draw your attention to where it says that on the 5th of July, 1995, members of the MUP of Serbia were brought to the surgical department in Srbanje and they are named. I will draw attention to one name. Under number 4, Miroslav Radisic [phoen], head injury, in a comma, serious bodily injury. Does this name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, the document is full of mistakes and incorrect information. There is a lot of incorrect information in this document. If you will allow me, I would like to draw your attention to number 1. The name is not Milorad Ristovic, but rather Milovan Ristic, who succumbed to his wounds. And under number 4, it is not Miroslav Radisic [phoen], but Radosic [phoen]. There is also another nonsense that I notice here. A journalist, an RTV journalist, was also apparently seriously wounded. This is nonsense. The entire text is completely wrong. I don't know who this chief of centre was, but it seems to be an illiterate person who was not privy to much information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, thank you. I would like to invite your comments about the things that I ask you to comment. Please do not misunderstand me. I'm not criticising you. I just need to be focussed in view of the time. Do you know that Ristic, Milorad [as interpreted] and Radosic, Milorad [as interpreted] were wounded and died? Did you receive information from Kajman how they died? And who else was injured?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it was in the course of the shelling, and the journalist of the radio/television in Serbia was also wounded together with them. He had been sent on an assignment there by Serbian television.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pelevic. Let's have a look at 2D905 now. This is a document that you provided to the Defence during the winter recess. Let's please have a look at the first page of this document. There's a request to provide a statement relating to Radosic Miroslav. Can you tell us what this is about, in fact? Let's just wait for the translation to appear for the Chamber. We have it now. Be so kind as to tell us what sort of a document this is. We can see that it's addressed to you, Borislav Pelevic.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, this requires an introduction, with your leave. Since the Republika Srbija, the Republic of Serbia, never took care of a single wounded person or the families of anyone who had been wounded or killed, they never provided pensions or any other form of assistance, these familiars and wounded individuals would claim their rights through the Government of the Republika Srpska. That's the case today. So I'm constantly in contact with him, and for five or six families I've already managed to obtain assistance. Because Republika Srpska, on the basis of my statements and other relevant documents, provided them with compensation, pensions, because their children were killed in the liberation of Republika Srpska. So all the rights of the members of the guards would be obtained through Republika Srpska and its Ministry of Labour, not through our country, not through Serbia. This is a document -- can I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'll put that question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may we move on to the following page. May we see the next page, please. It says Professor Borislav Pelevic. It's a statement from Professor Borislav Pelevic. It's the third page in the English version, Your Honour. I do apologise. Just to avoid any confusion: The second page in the B/C/S version and the third page in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You gave this statement. It concerned the circumstances under which this person was killed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Who did you send this statement to?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement was sent to the Ministry of Labour and Welfare Issues of the Government of Republika Srpska. I co-operate with them in order to take care of the families of killed members of the SDG, members of the SDG who were killed in the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You gave the statement on the 10th of February, 2011. Do you know whether anything was done on the basis of the statement, whether anything was obtained?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The mother of a combatant killed in action received a pension.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: From whom?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Government of Republika Srpska, from the Ministry for Labour and Combatants Welfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] [microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I suggest that this document be admitted into evidence, 2D905.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I see there's two pages that haven't been referenced to. But is the Defence tendering all four pages or just the two that have been referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it concerns all four pages, but I didn't want to use up more time. Time is limited for me in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If it could be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- it's a relatively short document, so therefore perhaps for reasons of context we should have all four pages in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2D905 will receive number D662, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let's have a look at 2D906 now. This concerns some other individual. And here we also have a response, a letter, from the Government of Republika Srpska. The individual concerned is Sasa Tomic. Could we please have a look at the last page in both the B/C/S and English version. This, Your Honours, is another example that relates to a different combatant. This document shows that it's an exchange between Republika Srpska and the Ministry for the Welfare of Veterans. It's an exchange between them and Borislav Pelevic, in fact. Could 2D906 already be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2D906 will receive number D663, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, we spoke about two individuals who were killed, and you said -- or you provided an explanation of the letter. Let's now have a look at a report dated the 23rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1470 is the exhibit number. And could we please see the first page. Could we see the first page of the typed document as well because there is a handwritten attachment to this document. This is a dispatch.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] [microphone not activated] ... we have no other documents in e-court, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's the third page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar, your microphone was not activated. We only read on the transcript: "Documents in e-court."

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: What is said, Your Honours, is that there are no other documents than those that are shown on the screen, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I've caused some confusion. We have the third page there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Have a look at the item under number 6. This is a report from General-Major Dragomir Milosevic. And under 6 it says something about combat operations: "In the course of combat, we sustained losses." And he also mentions two other combatants from part of the Serbian -- from a part of the Serbian Republic of Krajina. And he refers to volunteers. Are you aware of two volunteers from the Serbian Republic of Krajina being killed at a somewhat later date?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 6 on the -- it's -- the second page, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was thinking about two volunteers from the Serbian Republic of Krajina, but there was a -- some confusion here. The third individual, Radosic, was wounded. We've already spoken about him. He was taken to Belgrade to be treated there, but he died a few days later. So three combatants were in fact killed. But at the time he had information according to which only two volunteers from the Republic of Serbian Krajina were killed. So these were volunteers, volunteers of ours, from the SDG, the Serbian Volunteer Guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: My question is: Do you have any information according to which some soldiers, some volunteers from the Serbian Republic of Krajina were later killed? Because the date here mentioned is the 23rd of July, and combat during that period of time is referred to.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I refer the Chamber to Exhibit D207 which relates to this evidence. This is a report from the state of Serbia and concerns the names of all individuals who are mentioned in telegrams as members of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, we do have to move on. Please tell me, Did the SDG participate in combat in the Banja Luka Krajina?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you are referring to the period from September, October 1995, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could you tell me which forces the SDG participated in combat -- with which forces the SDG participated in combat in that terrain, in that field?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are about 200 seasoned volunteers from the SDG. They were under the command of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you also have occasion to go to that battle-field? And if so, when, and how much time did you spend there?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did visit the guards and the guards' commander when the Muslim and Croat forces acted together with the NATO support and they attacked Cadjevica, which was the first line in the direction of the Muslim army in the direction of the 5th Corps. So I visited the SDG, the Serbian Volunteer Guards, and Commander Arkan for five or six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know which other forces -- or in fact, first of all tell me, Do you know which period it was when you were there?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was after the 10th of October. I know that because that's when the guards celebrate their anniversary. I gave a speech in Erdut since the commander was at the Banja Luka battle-field. I don't know the exact date, but it was certainly sometime in mid-October.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, let's now have a look at D140. We have a telegram here from the deputy minister, Tomislav Kovac. It says: "On the basis of the decision of the president of the RS." And then we have the 17th of September, 1995. "On the decision of associating all the forces, we have formed a Joint Staff consisting of the representatives of the SVRS [as interpreted], the 1st Krajina Corps, the 2nd Krajina Corps, and the MUP." And under item 2, it says: "Raznjatovic, Zeljko." Are you aware of the fact that Arkan was part of some Joint Staff? And if you are aware of that fact, how did you find out about it?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was an order from the president of Republika Srpska, Radovan Karadzic, according to which all forces should join and should resist the enemy. All the units in the battle-field, in that battle-field, were under a Joint Command. One of the members of the staff was Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. Since our unit was very much respected, I found out about this when I visited the guards and Arkan and I saw that he was a member of the staff of the associated forces for -- of the Serbian army. In addition to our guards -- well, the Army of Republika Srpska played the main role, but there was also a brigade called the "vukovi," or the Wolves from Drina. This was a unit from Republika Srpska, a volunteer unit from Republika Srpska, which was part of these joint Serbian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since time is limited, I'd like to refer the Chamber to D28, P2948, and D82, which are exhibits that relate to these forces. Let's now have a look at --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Or, in fact, first of all, sir, tell me -- Mr. Pelevic, tell me, Did Arkan, together with his unit, receive combat orders? And, if so, from whom?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, received orders from Momir Talic, the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps, who was in charge of defence, and also from the minister of the interior of Republika Srpska, Tomislav Kovac, since he closely co-operated with the command of the special police brigade in Republika Srpska, Ljubomir or Ljubisa Borovcanin. I'm not quite sure what his first name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I refer the Chamber to D146, which is a combat order issued by Mr. Talic. In fact, I see there is a question mark there. Let's please have a look at the order. The exhibit number is D146. Could we have a look at the first page, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This is an order dated 13th of October, 1995. Is that the period during which you made that visit? We saw that Arkan was in the staff in Prijedor. We could see that in the previous document. We can see the command of the OD 10, Prijedor. And then the date, 13th of October, 1995. Under item 2 it says the OD 10 unit, and then it mentions its composition, the 15th Kozarska, LPGR [as interpreted], then it says detachment of the Serbian Volunteer Guards, the MUP, and 1 through 27, MTBR.

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is an order from General Momir Talic, the commander of the 1st Krajina Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: When you were there, could you observe co-operation between Mr. Talic and Arkan? Were orders given and received or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When Muslim and Croatian forces attacked, the commander and I went to Cadjevica, which was the front line, and there I also met General Talic. Since the Army of Republika Srpska started withdrawing towards Manjaca and towards Banja Luka as well, Momir Talic, Zeljko Raznjatovic, and myself went to return the troops because they were fleeing due to a false alarm. I spent the entire night with Momir Talic and Arkan. We managed to return the troops to their original positions and to stabilize the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, can you now look at 2D902. This is yet another photo that we received from you. Could you please tell us who are the individuals in the photo and where the photo was taken?

utterances.speaker: BORISLAV PELEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left-hand side you can see the minister of the police of Republika Srpska, Tomislav Kovac. And Commander Arkan is on the right-hand side. I took the photo myself in Manjaca. Manjaca is a hilltop between the front line in Cadjevica and Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we tender this document into evidence even before, but the source was challenged. Could I now have 2D902 admitted. The verso of this photo shows an inscription. The year 1995, Manjaca, near Banja Luka, Tomislav Kovac, Minister of the RSK MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no objection to the admission of the photograph. However, right now there's no foundation for what the writing is that follows on the subsequent page or the envelope on the last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps you can ask the witness whether he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the source was in dispute. The origin of the photo was in dispute. I don't need anything else to be admitted but the photo. I'm not relying on the inscription behind the photo or the envelope. Mr. Pelevic sent the photo to me, and he has just confirmed the origin of the photo and where it was taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Pelevic, could you tell us whose handwriting it is at the back of this photograph? And perhaps could we move to the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be displayed for me, please. I really don't know. This is not my handwriting. I gave a copy of this photo to Arkan and another copy to Tomo Kovac. This is not my handwriting. However, I took it and it belongs to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You took the photograph. You provided it to Mr. Bakrac, if I understand you well. Did you then give it to someone else? I mean, any idea on -- on how this handwriting appears on the back of the photograph? If it's not yours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I gave a copy of the photo to Commander Arkan, to Tomo Kovac, and to some other people perhaps. I don't remember. It was a long time ago. I really don't know how this could have happened, how anybody could have written on it. I have sorted all of my photos. I don't have that much time to write anything on the back of any of the photos. It may even be the handwriting of my wife. But in any case, the photograph depicts Tomo Kovac and Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you seriously telling us that you do not find the time, being so busy, that you could write three lines on the back of a photograph, Mr. Pelevic; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at that time, in addition to all of my duties and tasks, I was also the editor-in-chief of the Serbian Unity magazine that was published --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there before you explain to us how many difficult tasks you had to fulfil at the time. Apparently, from the start of your answer, that is what your evidence is; that you did not find the time to even -- and that explains why it could not be your handwriting, because you were too busy to write three lines at the back of a photograph. Is that your evidence? A simple yes or no would do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could I please be allowed to explain very briefly?
